tool.name: Flutter
tool.tagline: Google's UI toolkit for natively compiled apps from one Dart codebase
tool.description: Flutter is an open-source UI framework that renders every pixel itself, so one Dart codebase produces fast, consistent apps for iOS, Android, web, Windows, macOS and Linux. UIs are built from composable widgets, with hot reload for instant feedback. Learn it to ship polished cross-platform mobile apps with a single team and codebase.

concepts.name: Project setup and hot reload
concepts.summary: Create a Flutter project, understand its folders and main(), run it on a device, and use hot reload and hot restart.
concepts.why: The edit-reload loop is Flutter's superpower, and knowing the project layout saves hours of confusion.
concepts.body:
Install the Flutter SDK (it bundles Dart), then check your setup with `flutter doctor`, which reports missing Android, Xcode or browser toolchains.

`flutter create my_app` generates a project:

- `lib/main.dart` — your Dart code; `main()` calls `runApp(MyApp())`.
- `pubspec.yaml` — dependencies, assets and fonts.
- `android/`, `ios/`, `web/`, `macos/`... — thin native host projects you rarely touch.
- `test/` — tests.

`flutter run` builds and launches on a connected device, emulator, simulator or Chrome (`-d chrome`); `flutter devices` lists targets. IDE plug-ins for VS Code and Android Studio do the same with a debugger.

In debug mode the app runs on the Dart VM with a JIT, which enables:

- **Hot reload** (`r` in the terminal, or save in the IDE): injects changed code and rebuilds the widget tree while **keeping state**. Takes under a second.
- **Hot restart** (`R`): restarts the app and resets state; needed after changing `main()`, global initializers, enum declarations or a class from stateless to stateful.

Debug builds are slow and large on purpose. Measure performance only with `flutter run --profile`, and ship with `flutter build apk`, `appbundle`, `ipa` or `web`, which compile AOT.

`flutter pub add <package>` adds dependencies from pub.dev, just like `dart pub`.
takeaways: `main()` calls `runApp` with your root widget
Hot reload keeps state; hot restart resets it
Judge performance only in profile or release builds
pitfalls: Expecting hot reload to pick up changes to `main()` or static initializers — use hot restart.

quiz.q: You changed a widget's build method and want to see it without losing the current screen state. What do you use?
options: A full rebuild with flutter build
quiz.explain: Hot reload injects the new code and rebuilds widgets while keeping State objects.

concepts.name: Widgets and StatelessWidget
concepts.summary: Build UIs by composing immutable widgets, write StatelessWidgets, and understand build methods and BuildContext.
concepts.why: In Flutter everything on screen is a widget, so this mental model underlies every other lesson.
concepts.body:
A **widget** is an immutable description of part of the UI: text, padding, a button, a whole screen. You build interfaces by **composing** small widgets into a tree: a `Scaffold` contains a `Column`, which contains `Text` and `ElevatedButton` widgets, and so on.

A **`StatelessWidget`** depends only on its constructor arguments. You override `build(BuildContext context)` and return a widget tree. Flutter calls `build` whenever the widget is inserted or its inputs change, and may call it often, so keep it fast and side-effect free.

Conventions:

- Fields are `final`, and the constructor is `const` when possible: `const Greeting({super.key, required this.name});`. Passing `super.key` lets parents give the widget a key.
- Child widgets go in `child` or `children` named parameters.
- Extract a widget class when a build method grows; prefer new widget classes over helper methods returning widgets, since classes can be `const` and rebuild independently.

**`BuildContext`** is the widget's location in the tree. Use it to look up inherited data: `Theme.of(context)`, `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)`, `Navigator.of(context)`.

Because widgets are immutable and cheap, "changing" the UI means building new widgets with new values. Flutter diffs them against the previous tree and updates only what changed on screen.
takeaways: UIs are trees of small, immutable widgets
StatelessWidget = output depends only on constructor fields
Use `const` constructors and extract widget classes
pitfalls: Doing work with side effects (network calls, timers) inside `build`, which may run many times.

quiz.q: What should a StatelessWidget's build method depend on?
options: A counter it increments on each build
Its final fields and data looked up through BuildContext
quiz.explain: build must be a pure function of the widget's configuration and inherited data, because it can run at any time.

concepts.name: Row, Column, Container and padding
concepts.summary: Arrange widgets with Row, Column, Stack, Container, Padding, SizedBox and alignment properties.
concepts.why: Every screen is a combination of these few layout widgets.
concepts.body:
Flutter layout is done with widgets, not a separate style language.

- **`Column`** stacks children vertically, **`Row`** horizontally. `mainAxisAlignment` positions children along the main axis (`start`, `center`, `spaceBetween`, `spaceEvenly`...), `crossAxisAlignment` along the other. `mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min` shrinks the Row/Column to fit its children.
- **`Padding`** adds space inside, with `EdgeInsets.all(8)`, `.symmetric(horizontal: 16)` or `.only(top: 4)`.
- **`SizedBox`** gives a fixed size, and `SizedBox(height: 12)` is the idiomatic spacer. `Row` and `Column` also accept a `spacing:` parameter (Flutter 3.27+) to space children evenly.
- **`Center`** and **`Align`** position a single child.
- **`Container`** combines padding, margin, size, color, decoration (borders, rounded corners, shadows via `BoxDecoration`) and alignment. Use the specific widget when you only need one of these.
- **`Stack`** layers children on top of each other; `Positioned` places a child at offsets inside it, which is useful for badges and overlays.
- **`Expanded`** inside a Row or Column makes a child take the remaining space (covered with constraints next).

Turn on the **Widget Inspector** in DevTools or your IDE to see each widget's bounds; "Show guidelines" makes padding and alignment visible.

When a Row's children are too wide, you get the yellow-and-black overflow stripes — a sign to wrap a child in `Expanded` or `Flexible`, or make it scroll.
takeaways: Column/Row lay out along a main axis; set main and cross alignment
Padding, SizedBox, Center, Align for spacing and placement
Stack + Positioned for overlays
pitfalls: Using Container for everything — specific widgets like Padding and SizedBox are clearer.

quiz.q: Which property spaces a Column's children evenly from top to bottom?
quiz.explain: For a Column the main axis is vertical, and spaceEvenly distributes free space between and around children.

concepts.name: StatefulWidget and setState
concepts.summary: Keep mutable UI state in a State object, update it with setState, and use initState and dispose.
concepts.why: Any widget that changes in response to the user — a counter, a toggle, a text field — starts here.
concepts.body:
A **`StatefulWidget`** is split into two classes:

- The widget itself, still immutable, holding configuration.
- A **`State<T>`** object, created by `createState()`, which holds mutable data and builds the UI. Flutter keeps the State alive across rebuilds as long as the widget stays at the same place in the tree.

To change the UI, mutate the state inside **`setState(() { ... })`**. That marks the widget dirty so Flutter calls `build` again on the next frame. Changing a field without `setState` updates the value but not the screen.

Lifecycle methods on `State`:

- `initState()` — runs once when the State is created; set up controllers, subscriptions and animations here (call `super.initState()` first).
- `didUpdateWidget(oldWidget)` — the parent rebuilt with new configuration; react to changed fields.
- `dispose()` — release controllers, cancel subscriptions and timers (call `super.dispose()` last).

Inside State, the widget's fields are available through `widget.someField`, and `context` and `mounted` are properties. After an `await`, check `if (!mounted) return;` before calling `setState` or using `context`, because the widget may have been removed meanwhile.

Keep state as low in the tree as possible: only the widget that owns the state rebuilds. When several widgets need the same state, lift it up or use a state-management approach.
takeaways: Mutable data lives in a State object that survives rebuilds
Change it inside `setState` to trigger a rebuild
Set up in `initState`, clean up in `dispose`, check `mounted` after awaits
pitfalls: Calling `setState` after an `await` when the widget has been disposed — check `mounted` first.

quiz.q: You update a State field without calling setState. What happens?
options: The UI updates on the next frame anyway
The value changes but the widget isn't rebuilt, so the screen stays stale
quiz.explain: setState is what schedules a rebuild; without it the new value isn't shown until something else rebuilds.

concepts.name: MaterialApp, Scaffold and theming
concepts.summary: Structure screens with MaterialApp and Scaffold, and style the app consistently with ThemeData, ColorScheme and text themes.
concepts.why: A consistent theme makes the app look professional and lets you support dark mode and branding in one place.
concepts.body:
**`MaterialApp`** sets up the app: theme, localization, navigation and the home screen. (`CupertinoApp` is the iOS-styled alternative; most apps use Material and adapt where needed.)

**`Scaffold`** provides the standard screen structure: `appBar`, `body`, `floatingActionButton`, `drawer`, `bottomNavigationBar` / `NavigationBar`, and it hosts SnackBars via `ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(...)`.

Flutter uses **Material 3** by default. Build a theme from one seed color:

```dart
theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal)),
darkTheme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(
    seedColor: Colors.teal, brightness: Brightness.dark)),
themeMode: ThemeMode.system,
```

Widgets read the theme through `Theme.of(context)`: use `colorScheme.primary`, `colorScheme.surface`, and text styles like `textTheme.headlineSmall` instead of hard-coded colors and font sizes. Then dark mode and rebranding work automatically.

Customize components globally with component themes in `ThemeData`, e.g. `filledButtonTheme`, `inputDecorationTheme`, `cardTheme`. Override locally by wrapping a subtree in `Theme(data: ..., child: ...)` or passing a `style`.

Custom fonts are declared in `pubspec.yaml` and set with `fontFamily` or a text theme. Respect the user's text scaling: avoid fixed heights that clip enlarged text.
takeaways: MaterialApp configures theme and navigation; Scaffold structures a screen
Derive colors with `ColorScheme.fromSeed`; support dark mode with `darkTheme`
Read colors and text styles from `Theme.of(context)`
pitfalls: Hard-coding colors throughout widgets, which breaks dark mode and rebranding.

quiz.q: Where should a widget get its primary color so that dark mode works automatically?
quiz.explain: The ColorScheme from the active theme changes with light and dark themes, so reading it adapts automatically.

concepts.name: ListView and scrolling
concepts.summary: Show scrollable content with SingleChildScrollView, ListView, ListView.builder, separators and GridView.
concepts.why: Feeds, chats, settings and search results are all lists, and building them lazily keeps apps fast.
concepts.body:
Content taller than the screen must scroll.

- **`SingleChildScrollView`** makes one child (often a `Column`) scrollable. Fine for forms and short pages; it builds everything at once.
- **`ListView(children: [...])`** — a scrolling list of a fixed set of widgets, also built eagerly.
- **`ListView.builder(itemCount: n, itemBuilder: (context, i) => ...)`** builds items **lazily**, only those near the viewport. Use it for long or unbounded lists; thousands of items cost no more than a screenful.
- **`ListView.separated`** adds a separator widget between items.
- **`GridView.builder`** with a `SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount` or `...MaxCrossAxisExtent` for grids.

`ListTile` is a ready-made row with `leading`, `title`, `subtitle`, `trailing` and `onTap`.

Scroll behavior: control position with a `ScrollController` (create in `initState`, dispose in `dispose`), listen for the end of the list to load more, and use `RefreshIndicator` for pull-to-refresh.

A classic error: putting a `ListView` directly inside a `Column`. The list wants infinite height and the Column offers unbounded height, causing "Vertical viewport was given unbounded height". Wrap the list in `Expanded` so it gets the remaining space. Avoid `shrinkWrap: true` on long lists — it defeats lazy building.

Give list items stable **keys** when items can be reordered or removed.
takeaways: `ListView.builder`/`separated` build items lazily — use them for long lists
A ListView inside a Column needs `Expanded`
ListTile is the standard row; GridView.builder for grids
pitfalls: Using `shrinkWrap: true` on a long list inside another scroll view, which builds every item.

quiz.q: Why use ListView.builder for a list of 10,000 messages?
options: It builds only the items near the visible area
It is the only list that scrolls
quiz.explain: builder creates item widgets on demand as they scroll into view, keeping memory and build time low.

concepts.name: Buttons, text fields and gestures
concepts.summary: Handle taps with buttons and GestureDetector, read text with TextField and TextEditingController, and use switches and checkboxes.
concepts.why: Interactive apps need input, and controllers must be managed correctly to avoid leaks and lost text.
concepts.body:
**Buttons**: `FilledButton`, `ElevatedButton`, `OutlinedButton`, `TextButton` and `IconButton` take an `onPressed` callback. Pass `null` to show the button as disabled.

**Gestures** on arbitrary widgets: wrap them in `GestureDetector` (`onTap`, `onLongPress`, `onPanUpdate`...) or `InkWell` for a Material ripple.

**Text input** uses `TextField` (or `TextFormField` inside a form):

- `onChanged: (text) => ...` fires on every keystroke.
- A **`TextEditingController`** reads and sets the text programmatically: `controller.text`, `controller.clear()`. Create it in `initState` (or as a field) of a `State` and **dispose** it in `dispose`.
- `decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: ..., hintText: ..., errorText: ...)` styles it.
- `keyboardType`, `textInputAction`, `obscureText` for passwords, `autofocus`, and `onSubmitted`.
- A `FocusNode` controls focus; `FocusScope.of(context).unfocus()` hides the keyboard.

**Selection controls** are controlled widgets: `Switch(value: on, onChanged: (v) => setState(() => on = v))`, and likewise `Checkbox`, `Radio`, `Slider`, `DropdownMenu`. The widget shows whatever `value` you pass; it only *reports* changes, so you must store the new value and rebuild.

When the keyboard opens, `Scaffold` resizes its body by default; put forms in a scroll view so fields aren't hidden.
takeaways: `onPressed: null` disables a button
Controllers are created in State and disposed in `dispose`
Switches, checkboxes and sliders are controlled: store the value and rebuild
pitfalls: Creating a TextEditingController inside `build`, which resets the text on every rebuild and leaks.

quiz.q: A Switch's onChanged handler is `(v) {}` — what happens when the user taps it?
options: It appears not to change, because the value passed in never changes
quiz.explain: Switch is controlled: it displays the value you pass, so you must store the new value and call setState.

concepts.name: Images, icons and assets
concepts.summary: Declare assets in pubspec.yaml, show local and network images, and use icons and resolution-aware variants.
concepts.why: Logos, illustrations and avatars appear on almost every screen, and misconfigured assets are a common first bug.
concepts.body:
Files bundled with the app — images, JSON, fonts — are **assets**, declared in `pubspec.yaml`:

```yaml
flutter:
  assets:
    - assets/images/
    - assets/data/countries.json
```

Listing a directory includes its files (not subdirectories). After editing `pubspec.yaml`, do a full restart; hot reload doesn't pick up new assets.

Showing images:

- `Image.asset('assets/images/logo.png', width: 120)`.
- `Image.network(url, fit: BoxFit.cover, loadingBuilder: ..., errorBuilder: ...)` — always provide an `errorBuilder` for network images. The `cached_network_image` package adds disk caching.
- `fit` controls scaling (`cover`, `contain`, `fill`...), like CSS `object-fit`.
- `CircleAvatar(backgroundImage: NetworkImage(url))` for avatars.

**Resolution variants**: put `2.0x/logo.png` and `3.0x/logo.png` next to `logo.png`, and Flutter picks the right one for the device pixel ratio.

**Icons**: `Icon(Icons.home)` uses the bundled Material Icons font; `cupertino_icons` provides iOS-style ones. SVGs need the `flutter_svg` package.

Read text assets with `await rootBundle.loadString('assets/data/countries.json')` (from `package:flutter/services.dart`).

Decoding big images costs memory: pass `cacheWidth`/`cacheHeight` to decode at display size for thumbnails.
takeaways: Declare assets in `pubspec.yaml`, then hot restart
Always give network images an `errorBuilder`
Use 2.0x/3.0x variants and `cacheWidth` for crisp, memory-friendly images
pitfalls: Forgetting to list the asset folder in `pubspec.yaml`, causing "Unable to load asset".

quiz.q: You added assets/images/ to pubspec.yaml, but files in assets/images/icons/ aren't found. Why?
options: Listing a directory doesn't include its subdirectories
quiz.explain: Each subdirectory must be listed separately in the assets section.

concepts.name: Constraints, Expanded and Flexible
concepts.summary: Understand Flutter's rule that constraints go down, sizes go up and parents set position, and fix overflow and unbounded errors.
concepts.why: Almost every confusing layout bug is explained by the constraint model.
concepts.body:
Flutter layout follows one rule: **constraints go down, sizes go up, parent sets position**.

1. A parent passes each child **constraints**: a min and max width and height.
2. The child picks its own size within those constraints and reports it up.
3. The parent decides where to place the child.

Consequences:

- A widget can't choose any size it wants — only one inside its constraints. `Container(width: 100)` directly inside the screen fills the screen, because the screen forces **tight** constraints. Wrap it in `Center` or `Align` to loosen them.
- A widget doesn't know its position, and can't size itself relative to the screen without being told.

In a `Row` or `Column`, non-flexible children get **unbounded** space along the main axis: they're asked to be as big as they like. Then:

- **`Expanded(child: ...)`** forces the child to fill the leftover space, divided by `flex` factors.
- **`Flexible(child: ...)`** lets the child be *at most* its share (`FlexFit.loose`).
- Text that would overflow a Row should be in `Expanded` or `Flexible` with `overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis`.

Errors decoded:

- "RenderFlex overflowed by N pixels" — children are larger than the Row/Column; make one flexible or scrollable.
- "Viewport was given unbounded height" — a scrollable inside a Column; give it bounded height with `Expanded` or `SizedBox`.
- "BoxConstraints forces an infinite width" — a widget that wants to be infinitely wide inside an unbounded parent.

`LayoutBuilder` exposes the incoming constraints so you can choose a layout from the available space.
takeaways: Constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent positions
Expanded fills leftover space by `flex`; Flexible may be smaller
Center/Align loosen tight constraints so explicit sizes apply
pitfalls: Fixing overflow by hard-coding widths, which breaks on other screen sizes.

quiz.q: Why does `Container(width: 100, height: 100, color: Colors.red)` as the app's root fill the whole screen?
options: The screen passes tight constraints, so the child must be exactly screen-sized
It's a bug in debug mode
quiz.explain: The root receives tight constraints equal to the screen; the child can only choose a size within them.

concepts.name: Navigation and routing
concepts.summary: Move between screens with Navigator push and pop, pass arguments and results, and use go_router for URL-based routing and deep links.
concepts.why: Every multi-screen app needs navigation, and deep links and web URLs require declarative routing.
concepts.body:
The **`Navigator`** manages a stack of routes (screens).

- `Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailScreen(id: 3)))` shows a new screen; arguments are just constructor parameters.
- `Navigator.pop(context, result)` returns to the previous screen, optionally with a value. `push` returns a `Future` that completes with that result, so `final picked = await Navigator.push(...)` works for pickers.
- `pushReplacement` swaps the current screen (e.g. after login); `pushAndRemoveUntil` clears the stack.
- `showDialog` and `showModalBottomSheet` also push routes and return futures.

This imperative API is fine for simple apps. For **deep links**, web URLs, redirects (auth guards) and nested navigation such as bottom tabs that keep their own stacks, use a declarative router. The Flutter team maintains **`go_router`**:

```dart
final router = GoRouter(routes: [
  GoRoute(path: '/', builder: (c, s) => const HomeScreen()),
  GoRoute(path: '/item/:id', builder: (c, s) =>
      ItemScreen(id: s.pathParameters['id']!)),
]);
MaterialApp.router(routerConfig: router);
```

Navigate with `context.go('/item/42')` (replace the stack to match the URL) or `context.push('/item/42')` (add on top). `redirect` implements login guards, and `StatefulShellRoute` keeps per-tab stacks.

On Android, `PopScope` intercepts the system back gesture, e.g. to confirm discarding a draft. After awaiting a pushed route, check `context.mounted` before using `context` again.
takeaways: `push` returns a Future completed by `pop(context, result)`
Pass data to screens through constructor parameters
Use go_router for URLs, deep links, redirects and tab stacks
pitfalls: Using `context` after awaiting a route without checking `context.mounted`.

quiz.q: What does `await Navigator.push(...)` return?
options: The value passed to Navigator.pop for that route (or null)
quiz.explain: push returns a Future that completes with the result given to pop when that route is closed.

concepts.name: Forms and validation
concepts.summary: Group fields in a Form with a GlobalKey, validate with validator functions, and submit safely.
concepts.why: Sign-up, checkout and settings screens all need validated input with clear error messages.
concepts.body:
A **`Form`** groups `TextFormField`s (and other `FormField`s) so you can validate and save them together. Give the form a **`GlobalKey<FormState>`** stored in a `State` object, so you can reach the form's state from a button.

Each `TextFormField` takes a **`validator`**: a function that receives the current value (`String?`) and returns an error message, or `null` when valid. On submit:

```dart
if (_formKey.currentState!.validate()) {
  _formKey.currentState!.save();
  // send data
}
```

`validate()` runs every validator, shows the messages under the fields and returns whether all passed. `onSaved` callbacks then copy values into your model when you call `save()`.

UX details:

- `autovalidateMode: AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction` validates each field after the user first edits it, instead of only on submit.
- Use `keyboardType: TextInputType.emailAddress`, `textInputAction: TextInputAction.next` and `autofillHints` for faster input.
- Disable the submit button while a request is in flight and show progress.
- Server-side errors (e.g. "email already taken") can be shown by storing them in state and returning them from the validator, or via `InputDecoration.errorText`.

Keep validation logic in plain Dart functions so it's easy to unit test. Wrap the form in a `SingleChildScrollView` so the keyboard doesn't hide fields.
takeaways: A GlobalKey<FormState> lets you call validate() and save()
Validators return an error string or null
Keep validation in plain functions you can unit test
pitfalls: Creating the GlobalKey inside `build`, which makes a new form state on every rebuild.

quiz.q: What should a TextFormField validator return when the input is valid?
quiz.explain: Returning null means no error; any string is shown as the error message.

concepts.name: FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder
concepts.summary: Show loading, data and error states for asynchronous work with FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder, without refetching on every build.
concepts.why: Every screen that loads data must handle loading and failure gracefully.
concepts.body:
**`FutureBuilder<T>`** rebuilds when a future completes, and **`StreamBuilder<T>`** whenever a stream emits. Both call your `builder(context, snapshot)` with an **`AsyncSnapshot`**:

- `snapshot.connectionState` — `none`, `waiting`, `active` (streams) or `done`.
- `snapshot.hasData` / `snapshot.data`.
- `snapshot.hasError` / `snapshot.error`.

A typical builder returns a progress indicator while waiting, an error view on error, and the content otherwise. Dart 3 patterns make this tidy: `switch (snapshot) { AsyncSnapshot(hasError: true) => ..., AsyncSnapshot(:final data?) => ..., _ => spinner }`.

The most common bug: creating the future **inside `build`**:

```dart
FutureBuilder(future: api.fetchUser(), ...) // refetches on every rebuild!
```

Any rebuild — a theme change, keyboard opening, parent `setState` — starts a new request and flashes the spinner. Instead, create the future once in `initState` (or in a view model) and store it in a field. To refresh, assign a new future inside `setState`.

`StreamBuilder` subscribes and unsubscribes automatically as the widget enters and leaves the tree. Pass `initialData` to avoid a flicker when you already have a value.

For more complex apps, keep async loading in a state-management layer and expose simple states (loading, data, error) to widgets; `FutureBuilder` is ideal for small, local cases.
takeaways: Handle waiting, error and data states from AsyncSnapshot
Create the future once (initState or a field), never in `build`
Refresh by assigning a new future in `setState`
pitfalls: Calling the fetch function directly in the `future:` argument, re-running it on every rebuild.

quiz.q: Why is `FutureBuilder(future: http.get(url), ...)` written directly in build a bug?
options: Each rebuild starts a new request and resets the snapshot to waiting
quiz.explain: build runs often, so the future must be created once and reused across rebuilds.

concepts.name: HTTP requests and JSON models
concepts.summary: Call REST APIs with package:http, decode JSON into typed model classes, and handle status codes and errors.
concepts.why: Nearly every app talks to a backend, and typed models catch API mismatches early.
concepts.body:
Add the official **`http`** package (`flutter pub add http`) and call `http.get(Uri.parse(url))`, `http.post(uri, headers: ..., body: jsonEncode(data))`. Each returns a `Future<Response>` with `statusCode` and `body`. Check the status yourself; `http` doesn't throw on 404 or 500. Network failures throw (e.g. `SocketException`, or `ClientException`).

Decode with `jsonDecode(response.body)` from `dart:convert`. The result is untyped (`Map<String, dynamic>` or `List<dynamic>`), so convert it to **model classes** at the boundary:

- A `factory User.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json)` constructor, ideally using Dart 3 map patterns to check types: `{'id': int id, 'name': String name}`.
- A `toJson()` method for sending.

For larger models, code generation with `json_serializable` (plus `build_runner`) or `freezed` writes this boilerplate for you.

Good practices:

- Keep HTTP code out of widgets, in a repository or service class that returns models and throws domain errors.
- Use a single `http.Client` and close it when done; it reuses connections.
- Add timeouts: `.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10))`.
- Decode very large JSON off the UI thread with `compute` or `Isolate.run`.
- On Android, release builds need the `INTERNET` permission in the manifest; macOS apps need the network client entitlement.

`dio` is a popular alternative with interceptors, cancellation and progress callbacks.
takeaways: Check `statusCode` yourself — http doesn't throw on 4xx/5xx
Convert JSON to typed models at the boundary, e.g. with map patterns
Keep HTTP in a service/repository, not in widgets
pitfalls: Using `json['field']` dynamically throughout the UI, so API changes crash at run time far from the cause.

quiz.q: A server returns status 500. What does `await http.get(uri)` do?
quiz.explain: package:http only throws for transport errors; HTTP error statuses come back as normal responses.

concepts.name: Shared state: ChangeNotifier and Provider
concepts.summary: Lift state up, share it with InheritedWidget, model it with ChangeNotifier, and use provider or Riverpod for app-wide state.
concepts.why: Once several screens need the same data, setState alone becomes unmanageable.
concepts.body:
`setState` is ideal for **ephemeral** state used by one widget. **App state** — the signed-in user, a cart, settings — is needed by many widgets across screens.

Step one is **lifting state up**: move it to the closest common ancestor and pass data and callbacks down. This works but leads to "prop drilling" through many layers.

Flutter's built-in solution for passing data down is **`InheritedWidget`**: descendants call `context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType<T>()` (usually wrapped in a static `of(context)`), and they're rebuilt automatically when it changes. `Theme.of` and `MediaQuery.of` work this way.

To model changing state, use a **`ChangeNotifier`**: a class that holds data, exposes methods that mutate it and calls `notifyListeners()`. Widgets rebuild via `ListenableBuilder`, or through packages:

- **provider** — wraps InheritedWidget. Provide with `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Cart(), child: ...)`; read with `context.watch<Cart>()` (rebuilds on change) or `context.read<Cart>()` (no rebuild, for callbacks); `context.select` rebuilds only when a chosen value changes.
- **Riverpod**, **Bloc/Cubit**, **signals** and others offer different trade-offs in testability and boilerplate.

The official architecture guide uses `ChangeNotifier` view models with `ListenableBuilder`. Whatever you pick, keep business logic out of widgets, keep state immutable where practical, and rebuild as small a subtree as possible.
takeaways: Ephemeral state: setState; shared app state: lift up or use a notifier
ChangeNotifier + notifyListeners models observable state
provider: `watch`/`select` to rebuild, `read` inside callbacks
pitfalls: Calling `context.watch` inside an `onPressed` callback — use `read` there.

quiz.q: In provider, which call should an onPressed callback use to add an item to the cart?
quiz.explain: read gets the object without subscribing to changes, which is what event handlers need.

concepts.name: Responsive and adaptive layouts
concepts.summary: Adapt layouts to screen size with MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder and breakpoints, and respect safe areas, orientation and platform conventions.
concepts.why: Flutter apps run on phones, tablets, foldables, desktops and the web, so one fixed layout isn't enough.
concepts.body:
**Responsive** means the layout adjusts to available space; **adaptive** means it adjusts to the device's input and conventions (mouse vs touch, iOS vs Android).

Tools for size:

- `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)` — the window size. Use the specific `sizeOf`, `paddingOf`, `orientationOf` methods rather than `MediaQuery.of(context)`, so the widget only rebuilds when that aspect changes.
- **`LayoutBuilder`** — gives the constraints from the parent, which is better for reusable components that may be placed in a side panel rather than full screen.
- Breakpoints, following Material 3 window size classes: compact below 600 dp wide, medium 600–839, expanded 840 and up. A compact layout might use `NavigationBar` at the bottom; wider ones a `NavigationRail` and two panes.

Other essentials:

- **`SafeArea`** keeps content clear of notches, status bars and home indicators.
- Flexible widgets (`Expanded`, `Wrap`, `GridView` with `maxCrossAxisExtent`) adapt better than fixed sizes.
- `OrientationBuilder` or the size itself for rotation.
- Text scaling: test with large fonts; don't fix heights around text.

Adaptive touches: `Theme.of(context).platform` or `defaultTargetPlatform` to choose platform-specific behavior, `.adaptive` constructors (`Switch.adaptive`, `CircularProgressIndicator.adaptive`), hover and keyboard shortcuts on desktop and web.

Don't lock the app to portrait unless there's a strong reason; Android large-screen guidance discourages it.
takeaways: Use `MediaQuery.sizeOf` for window size and LayoutBuilder for local space
Switch layouts at breakpoints (e.g. 600 and 840 dp)
Wrap content in SafeArea and test large text
pitfalls: Using `MediaQuery.of(context).size` everywhere, causing rebuilds on any media change such as the keyboard opening.

quiz.q: A reusable card should pick a layout based on the space its parent gives it, not the whole screen. What should it use?
quiz.explain: LayoutBuilder provides the parent's constraints, which reflect the space actually available to the widget.

concepts.name: The element tree, keys and State identity
concepts.summary: Learn how widgets map to elements, when State is kept or recreated, and how ValueKey, ObjectKey, UniqueKey and GlobalKey change that.
concepts.why: Bugs like state jumping to the wrong list item or text fields losing input come from not understanding element identity.
concepts.body:
Widgets are short-lived configurations. Behind them Flutter keeps a long-lived **element tree**: each widget in the tree is backed by an `Element`, and stateful elements own their `State` object.

On rebuild, Flutter walks the old elements and the new widgets side by side. For each position it asks `Widget.canUpdate(old, new)`: **same runtime type and same key**. If true, the element is reused and updated with the new widget — the State survives and `didUpdateWidget` runs. If false, the old element (and its State) is disposed and a new one is created.

Without keys, children of a `Column` or `ListView` are matched **by position**. Remove the first item of a list of stateful tiles and the State of the old first tile is now attached to what was the second item — checkboxes, text and animations appear to jump.

**Keys** fix identity:

- `ValueKey(todo.id)` — identity from a stable value; the usual choice for list items.
- `ObjectKey(obj)` — identity of an object instance.
- `UniqueKey()` — always new, forcing a fresh State every build (useful to reset a widget deliberately).
- `GlobalKey` — unique across the whole app; lets an element move between parents keeping its State, and gives access to `currentState` (as with forms). It's relatively expensive; use sparingly.

Keys only matter among **siblings** (except GlobalKey). Also note that wrapping a widget in a new parent conditionally (e.g. `if (x) Padding(child: w) else w`) changes the tree shape and recreates the State.
takeaways: Elements (and State) are reused when runtime type and key match
Unkeyed siblings are matched by position
Use ValueKey for list items; GlobalKey sparingly
pitfalls: Using `UniqueKey()` in a list item builder, which recreates every item's State on every rebuild.

quiz.q: Two widgets at the same position have the same type and key across rebuilds. What happens to the StatefulWidget's State?
options: It's moved to the end of the list
It's kept and the element is updated with the new widget
quiz.explain: canUpdate is true, so the existing element and its State are reused and didUpdateWidget is called.

concepts.name: Implicit and explicit animations
concepts.summary: Animate with implicit widgets like AnimatedContainer, build explicit animations with AnimationController and Tween, and use Hero transitions.
concepts.why: Motion makes apps feel polished and helps users follow changes, and Flutter makes it cheap to add.
concepts.body:
**Implicit animations** are the easy path: widgets such as `AnimatedContainer`, `AnimatedOpacity`, `AnimatedAlign`, `AnimatedPadding`, `AnimatedSwitcher` and `AnimatedCrossFade` animate automatically whenever their target properties change. Give them a `duration` and optional `curve`, then just change values with `setState`. `TweenAnimationBuilder` does the same for any value.

**Explicit animations** give full control — looping, reversing, staggering, driving by a gesture:

- An **`AnimationController`** produces values from 0.0 to 1.0 over a `duration`, ticking once per frame. It needs a `vsync`: mix `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` (or `TickerProviderStateMixin` for several controllers) into your State and pass `this`. Create it in `initState`, **dispose it** in `dispose`.
- Control it with `forward()`, `reverse()`, `repeat()`, `animateTo()`, `stop()`.
- A **`Tween`** maps 0–1 to a range: `Tween(begin: 0.0, end: 200.0).animate(CurvedAnimation(parent: controller, curve: Curves.easeOut))`.
- Rebuild with **`AnimatedBuilder`** (or transition widgets like `FadeTransition`, `SlideTransition`, `ScaleTransition`) so only the animated subtree rebuilds each frame.

**Hero** animates a shared element between routes: wrap both widgets in `Hero(tag: sameTag, child: ...)`.

Prefer transitions that animate opacity and transforms; they're cheap to render. Respect `MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context)` for users who reduce motion.
takeaways: Implicit `Animated*` widgets animate when their properties change
AnimationController + Tween + a transition/AnimatedBuilder for full control
Controllers need a TickerProvider mixin and must be disposed
pitfalls: Calling setState in an animation listener to rebuild the whole screen every frame instead of using AnimatedBuilder or a transition.

quiz.q: What does `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` provide to an AnimationController?
options: A vsync ticker that fires once per frame and pauses when the widget is not visible
quiz.explain: The mixin makes the State a TickerProvider so the controller ticks in sync with frames and is muted offscreen.

concepts.name: Unit, widget and integration tests
concepts.summary: Test logic with unit tests, UI with widget tests using WidgetTester and finders, and full flows with integration_test.
concepts.why: Widget tests run in milliseconds without a device and catch UI regressions before users do.
takeaways: Unit tests for logic, widget tests for UI, integration tests for full flows
`pumpWidget`, interact, then `pump()` before asserting
Find by key, text, type or icon; inject fakes instead of real HTTP
pitfalls: Forgetting `await tester.pump()` after a tap, so the expectation sees the old UI.

quiz.q: After `await tester.tap(...)` triggers setState, why call `await tester.pump()` before checking the text?
options: To render a new frame so the rebuilt UI is visible to finders
It's optional and has no effect
quiz.explain: The test environment only rebuilds when a frame is pumped, so pump applies the pending setState.

concepts.name: App architecture: layers, view models, DI
concepts.summary: Structure apps into UI, view models, repositories and services, inject dependencies, and keep data flowing one way.
concepts.why: Without clear layers, Flutter apps turn into giant widgets that are impossible to test or change.
concepts.body:
Flutter's official architecture guide recommends separating concerns into layers:

- **UI layer** — **views** (widgets) that display state and forward user events, and **view models** (often `ChangeNotifier`s) that hold UI state, expose commands, and convert domain data to what the view needs. Widgets contain no business logic.
- **Data layer** — **repositories** are the source of truth for each data type (users, orders): they combine services, cache, retry and convert raw data into domain models. **Services** wrap one external source: a REST API, local database, platform plugin. They're stateless.
- Optionally a **domain layer** of use cases when logic spans several repositories.

Data flows **one way**: services → repositories → view models → views. Events go the other way: the view calls a view-model method, which calls a repository, which updates state, which notifies the view.

**Dependency injection**: construct services and repositories once (at app start), and pass them into view models through constructors. Use `provider` (or Riverpod, `get_it`) to make them available to the widget tree. This makes every layer testable with fakes.

Other recommendations: immutable domain models (`freezed` helps), a `Result` type instead of throwing across layers, feature-based folders (`lib/ui/cart/`, `lib/data/repositories/`), and the **command pattern** for actions with running/error state.

Scale the structure to the app — a two-screen app doesn't need use cases.
takeaways: Views + view models (UI) and repositories + services (data)
Data flows one way; events flow back through view-model methods
Inject dependencies through constructors so layers can be faked in tests
pitfalls: Calling HTTP directly from widgets, which makes them untestable and duplicates logic.

quiz.q: In the recommended architecture, which layer should cache data and be the source of truth for it?
quiz.explain: Repositories own data for their type, combining services, caching and converting to domain models.

concepts.name: Slivers and custom scroll effects
concepts.summary: Compose scrollable areas from slivers with CustomScrollView, SliverAppBar, SliverList and SliverGrid.
concepts.why: Collapsing headers, mixed lists and grids, and sticky sections all require slivers.
concepts.body:
A **sliver** is a piece of a scrollable area that lays itself out lazily according to the scroll position. `ListView` and `GridView` are convenience wrappers around a single sliver. To mix several kinds of content in one scroll, use a **`CustomScrollView`** with a list of slivers:

- **`SliverAppBar`** — an app bar that can expand, collapse (`expandedHeight`, `flexibleSpace: FlexibleSpaceBar(...)`), stay `pinned`, or reappear when scrolling up (`floating`, `snap`).
- **`SliverList`** with `SliverChildBuilderDelegate`, or the convenient `SliverList.builder` / `SliverList.separated` — lazy lists.
- **`SliverGrid`** — lazy grids.
- **`SliverToBoxAdapter`** — wraps one ordinary (box) widget.
- **`SliverPadding`**, **`SliverFillRemaining`**, **`SliverPersistentHeader`** (custom sticky headers), and `PinnedHeaderSliver` / `SliverResizingHeader` in recent Flutter versions.

Only sliver widgets may be direct children of `slivers:`; putting a plain widget there throws. Box widgets go inside `SliverToBoxAdapter`, and large lists must stay as `SliverList` to remain lazy — never a `Column` in an adapter.

Slivers use **`SliverConstraints`** (scroll offset, remaining paint extent) instead of box constraints, and report a `SliverGeometry`. That's what lets them shrink, pin or disappear as you scroll.

`NestedScrollView` coordinates an outer header with inner scrollables, for example tabs under a collapsing app bar.
takeaways: CustomScrollView combines several slivers in one scroll
SliverAppBar gives collapsing, pinned and floating headers
Only slivers go in `slivers:`; wrap box widgets in SliverToBoxAdapter
pitfalls: Putting a big Column of items in a SliverToBoxAdapter, losing lazy building.

quiz.q: You need a normal Text widget between a SliverAppBar and a SliverList. How do you add it?
options: Use a Column around all slivers
quiz.explain: slivers only accepts sliver widgets; SliverToBoxAdapter wraps a single box widget as a sliver.

concepts.name: Three trees and the rendering pipeline
concepts.summary: Understand widgets, elements and render objects, the build-layout-paint-composite pipeline, and how Impeller draws frames.
concepts.why: Expert debugging and performance work requires knowing exactly what happens between setState and pixels.
concepts.body:
Flutter maintains **three trees**:

- **Widgets** — immutable configuration, rebuilt freely.
- **Elements** — the persistent instances that hold the tree structure, State, and inherited-widget dependencies. `BuildContext` *is* the element.
- **RenderObjects** — do layout, painting and hit testing. Only `RenderObjectWidget`s (like `Padding`, `Opacity`, `RichText`) create them; most widgets you write are compositions that produce none.

A frame, driven by the engine's vsync signal through `SchedulerBinding`:

1. **Animate** — tickers run and controllers update values.
2. **Build** — dirty elements (marked by `setState`, inherited changes) rebuild, top-down; elements are updated or replaced as described by keys and types.
3. **Layout** — render objects marked `needsLayout` lay out: constraints down, sizes up. **Relayout boundaries** stop propagation when a parent's size can't depend on the child.
4. **Paint** — render objects record drawing commands into **layers**. `RepaintBoundary` gives a subtree its own layer so it can repaint independently.
5. **Composite** — the layer tree becomes a scene sent to the engine.
6. **Rasterize** — on the raster thread, **Impeller** (the default renderer on iOS and Android) turns the scene into GPU commands. Impeller precompiles shaders at build time, removing the first-run shader-compilation jank of the old Skia backend.

The UI thread (Dart) and raster thread run in parallel, each with a budget of about 16 ms at 60 Hz (8 ms at 120 Hz). Semantics (accessibility) is a parallel tree built from render objects.
takeaways: Widgets configure, elements persist, render objects lay out and paint
Frame = animate, build, layout, paint, composite, rasterize
Impeller precompiles shaders, avoiding first-run jank
pitfalls: Assuming a rebuild always means a repaint — unchanged render objects skip layout and paint.

quiz.q: In the three-tree model, which object is a BuildContext?
quiz.explain: BuildContext is the interface implemented by Element, representing the widget's location in the tree.

concepts.name: Profiling and performance
concepts.summary: Find and fix jank with profile mode and DevTools, reduce rebuilds, use const and RepaintBoundary, and avoid expensive effects.
concepts.why: Smooth 60–120 fps scrolling and animation is what users notice, and fixes require measuring first.
concepts.body:
Always measure in **profile mode** (`flutter run --profile`) on a real, preferably low-end, device. Debug mode is much slower and misleading.

**DevTools** tools:

- **Performance view** — frame chart split into UI (build/layout/paint in Dart) and raster (GPU) time. Red frames exceeded the budget.
- **CPU profiler** — which Dart functions consume time.
- **Track widget rebuilds** and "Highlight repaints" to spot unnecessary work.
- **Memory view** — leaks and large allocations.

UI-thread fixes:

- Rebuild less: push state down, split big widgets, use `const` constructors (identical const widgets are skipped), and `context.select` / `ValueListenableBuilder` for narrow rebuilds.
- Keep `build` cheap; never parse JSON, sort large lists or do I/O in it. Move heavy CPU work to an isolate.
- Use lazy builders for lists and grids; avoid `shrinkWrap` and intrinsic sizing (`IntrinsicHeight`), which force extra layout passes.

Raster-thread fixes:

- Avoid `saveLayer` triggers: `Opacity` on large subtrees (use `FadeTransition` or color alpha instead), `ShaderMask`, `ColorFilter`, and clipping with anti-aliasing on animated content.
- Wrap frequently repainting areas (a spinner, a video) in `RepaintBoundary` so the rest isn't repainted.
- Size images to display size with `cacheWidth`.

Check app size with `flutter build apk --analyze-size` and startup with `--trace-startup`.
takeaways: Profile in profile mode on real devices with DevTools
Shrink rebuild scope; use const and narrow listeners
Avoid saveLayer-heavy effects; isolate repaints with RepaintBoundary
pitfalls: Optimizing blindly in debug mode without looking at the UI vs raster thread breakdown.

quiz.q: DevTools shows slow frames with the raster thread over budget but the UI thread fast. What's the most likely culprit?
options: Expensive painting effects such as Opacity or clips over large areas
quiz.explain: Raster time is GPU work from painting; saveLayer-triggering effects are a common cause, not Dart build work.

concepts.name: Platform channels, plugins and FFI
concepts.summary: Call native Android and iOS code with MethodChannel and EventChannel, generate type-safe bindings with Pigeon, and call C with dart:ffi.
concepts.why: When no plugin exists for a native API or SDK, you have to bridge to Kotlin, Swift or C yourself.
concepts.body:
Flutter apps reach native APIs in three ways:

**Plugins** from pub.dev (`camera`, `url_launcher`, `shared_preferences`...) wrap native code behind a Dart API. Check them first; federated plugins have separate packages per platform.

**Platform channels** pass asynchronous messages between Dart and the host (Kotlin/Java on Android, Swift/Objective-C on iOS):

- **`MethodChannel`** — request/response: Dart calls `await channel.invokeMethod<int>('getBattery')`; native code registers a handler and replies with a result or an error (which arrives as a `PlatformException`).
- **`EventChannel`** — a stream of events from native to Dart (sensors, connectivity).
- Messages use the `StandardMessageCodec`: null, bools, numbers, strings, byte arrays, lists and maps.
- Native handlers run on the platform's main thread by default; don't block it. Use background task queues for heavy work.

Stringly typed channel names and arguments are error-prone, so the Flutter team's **Pigeon** package generates type-safe Dart, Kotlin and Swift code from a Dart interface definition.

**`dart:ffi`** calls C functions directly and synchronously, without message passing — ideal for C libraries (SQLite, image codecs, crypto). `package:ffigen` generates bindings from headers, and build hooks / native assets can compile and bundle the C code. On iOS and macOS, FFI can also reach Objective-C and Swift via `ffigen`, and Java/Kotlin via `jnigen` on Android.

Platform views (`AndroidView`, `UiKitView`) embed native UI like maps, at some performance cost.
takeaways: MethodChannel for request/response, EventChannel for native event streams
Use Pigeon for type-safe channels instead of raw strings
dart:ffi calls C synchronously without channels
pitfalls: Doing slow work in a native channel handler on the platform main thread, freezing the app.

quiz.q: When is dart:ffi preferable to a MethodChannel?
options: When calling a Kotlin UI API
When calling a C library directly, synchronously and without message encoding
quiz.explain: FFI binds directly to C functions, avoiding asynchronous channel messaging and codecs.

concepts.name: CustomPainter and custom drawing
concepts.summary: Draw charts, gauges and custom shapes with CustomPaint and CustomPainter, repaint efficiently, and animate drawings.
concepts.why: When no widget fits the design, drawing on the canvas gives full control with excellent performance.
concepts.body:
**`CustomPaint`** hands you a **`Canvas`** to draw on through a **`CustomPainter`**:

- `paint(Canvas canvas, Size size)` draws using `canvas.drawLine`, `drawRect`, `drawRRect`, `drawCircle`, `drawArc`, `drawPath`, `drawImage`, and text via `TextPainter`. Coordinates start at the top-left of the given size.
- **`Paint`** objects describe style: `color`, `strokeWidth`, `style` (fill or stroke), `strokeCap`, `shader` for gradients, `maskFilter` for blur.
- **`Path`** builds complex shapes with `moveTo`, `lineTo`, `quadraticBezierTo`, `cubicTo`, `arcTo` and `addOval`, combined with `Path.combine`.
- `canvas.save()` / `restore()` with `translate`, `rotate`, `scale` transform drawing; `clipRect`/`clipPath` clip it.

**`shouldRepaint(oldDelegate)`** decides whether a new painter instance requires repainting; compare the inputs and return `false` when nothing changed.

For animation, pass the `Animation` (any `Listenable`) as the painter's **`repaint`** argument: `MyPainter(progress: controller) : super(repaint: controller)`. The painter then repaints on every tick **without rebuilding any widgets** — the most efficient way to animate a drawing.

Give `CustomPaint` a size via `size:` or a child or parent constraints; otherwise it may be zero-sized. Wrap it in `RepaintBoundary` if it repaints often. For hit testing on custom shapes, override `hitTest`. For accessibility, provide `semanticsBuilder` or wrap it in `Semantics` with a label, since the canvas has no semantic content.
takeaways: Draw with Canvas + Paint + Path in a CustomPainter
Pass an Animation as `repaint` to animate without rebuilding widgets
Implement `shouldRepaint` carefully and add semantics
pitfalls: Returning `true` from shouldRepaint unconditionally, repainting even when nothing changed.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of passing an AnimationController as a CustomPainter's `repaint` argument?
options: It caches the drawing as an image
The canvas repaints every tick without rebuilding the widget tree
quiz.explain: The painter listens to the Listenable and marks itself for repaint directly, skipping build and layout.
